images.caption: Figure 1:Overview of the RynnVLA-Latent pretraining corpus.We aggregate approximately 30.1K hours from 25 datasets, comprising 16.63M episodes and 3.057B frames. Human video and real-robot video each contribute approximately 40% of the duration, with simulation accounting for the remaining 20%. The figure summarizes source composition, dataset contributions by duration, and object and action vocabulary from public tasks.

Figure 2:Data curation pipeline.The video data is collected from diverse sources and partitioned into short clips during data preprocessing. Each clip undergoes a multi-modal annotation process: (1) Video Captioning: Qwen3-VL(Bai et al., 2025)generates detailed natural language descriptions of the video content; (2) Optical Flow Estimation: DPFlow(Morimitsu et al., 2025)computes dense per-frame motion fields; (3) Depth Estimation: Depth Anything 3(Lin et al., 2025)produces monocular depth predictions.

Figure 3:Architecture of RynnLAM and comparison with existing methods.(a)Conventional latent action models compress a frame transition into a single latent representation and reconstruct the future observation conditioned on the source frame.(b)RynnLAMfactorizes transition information into motion tokensztmz_{t}^{m}, an action latentztaz_{t}^{a}, and a camera latentztcz_{t}^{c}. The three components are trained through complementary objectives: feature-space reconstruction, 3D dynamic-flow prediction, and relative camera-pose estimation, respectively. This factorization encourages the action representation to capture physical scene dynamics while encouraging camera ego-motion to be represented separately.

Figure 4:Two-stage training pipeline of RynnVLA-Latent.(a) Latent-action pretraining.RynnLAM provides shared transition descriptors for human and heterogeneous robot videos. The policy predicts these descriptors from observations and language.(b) Robot post-training.Both the pretrained RynnBrain backbone and action-expert trunk are reused. The output projection is retargeted to native robot actions, and proprioceptive state is introduced. Post-training adapts the pretrained policy to the target control space without adding a separate latent-to-action decoder.

Figure 5:Standardized Experimental Platforms.Two dual-arm embodiments used for real-world evaluation: the stationaryMarvin-WUJI(dual 7-DOF arms with 20-DOF dexterous hands) and the mobileAstribot-S1(dual 7-DOF arms with parallel grippers on a wheeled base).

Figure 6:Latent-action similarity visualization.We retrieve the nearest neighbors of several query latent actions
across the multi-embodiment corpus and display the corresponding
video frames. The displayed high-similarity neighbors exhibit related motion patterns across different embodiments and visual domains, providing a qualitative illustration of cross-domain transition similarity.
Figure 7:Post-training evaluation on real-world tasks.Each row shows the language instruction and representative execution frames for one task on the corresponding platform.

Figure 9:Qualitative visualization of 3D scene flowdecoded from latent actions predicted by RynnVLA-Latent. Given the current observation and language instruction, RynnVLA-Latent predicts a latent-action chunk, which is fed into the RynnLAM flow decoder to visualize the implied 3D motion.
Figure 10:Marvin-WUJI demonstration collection.Motion trackers control the dual robot arms, and data gloves control the dexterous hands.
